P5n3: In the model I’m imagining, some of the functions that are outsourced to therapists in modern society are distributed throughout the community. In other words, there’s a lot of peer counseling going on, people listening to each other, being there for each other and helping each other process ordinary emotional stuff.
P7n1: I’m going to use the phrase “free resource,” which comes from Re-evaluation Counseling, to refer to the attention, steadiness, skill and practical capacity people have left over for others once they’ve dealt with enough of their own immediate stuff, and “need” to refer to the amount of help people need at a given time.
P11s1: The problem is that, in a group of eight people, if two are in a sustained crisis mode, the group may end up spending most of its attention caring for those in crisis. However, in a group of eighty people, the same need can often be spread across lots of relationships and practical roles. A group can only absorb as much need as its members have free resource to meet.
P12n1: So it’s partly a problem of resources, not compassion -- how many people can a group take in without hurting the existing members or the people they’ve promised to support?
P14n1: So early on, members usually need to have more resource than acute need, and some skill to contribute, and a willingness to learn.

P16f: This community may not be a good fit for you right now if:
L1w1: You’re running from some crisis right now and mainly need a place to land, get treatment, housing, legal aid, etc. (A founding group shouldn’t pretend it can replace those.)

P2f: This does not surprise me, since we are taught to put on a show of competence in modern society. We have a lot of incentives to hide ourselves in our lives and disappear behind our screens the second things get uncomfortable. We have been encouraged to be narrow in our skills, and then our institutions act surprised that when a conflict comes up, all anyone knows how to do is appoint a subcommittee or just hit block.
P13o1: There is a difficult paradox to consider. The need for new members in a small community is greater, but the ability of that community to tolerate the disruption of new members is less. Whether there are eight people in the community or eighty, someone still has to grow the food, fix the cars, balance the books, watch the kids, and maintain the water system. The water well doesn’t care how beautiful someone’s heart is.
